opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's a really interesting direction, partly because it sort of flips how we usually think about evaluation. Traditionally you'd have a single output, compare it to a gold reference, and score it. With reasoning models, you often generate many candidate chains of thought, and the question becomes: how do you pick the best one, or how do you even tell which ones are good?

What I find fascinating is that judging seems easier than generating. A model that might not reliably produce the right reasoning path on the first try can still look at, say, eight different attempts side by side and spot which ones are coherent, which ones skipped a step, which ones hallucinated something in the middle. That's a verification versus generation gap, and it's kind of a free lunch if you can exploit it well.

There's also the comparative aspect. Asking a judge "is this answer good?" in isolation is noisy, because absolute scoring is hard and the calibration drifts. But asking "which of these is better?" or "rank these" gives a much more stable signal. Humans work the same way. We're bad at saying something is a 7 out of 10 but pretty good at saying A is better than B.

Then of course there are the failure modes, which are just as interesting. Judges have biases: position bias, length bias, a tendency to prefer outputs that sound confident or look like their own style. With reasoning traces in particular, a long, very elaborate chain can look more "thoughtful" even when it's wrong. So there's this subtle risk where you end up optimizing for reasoning that looks good to the judge rather than reasoning that's actually correct. If you then feed that back into training, you can get a kind of reward hacking loop.

So for me it sits at this nice intersection of evaluation, inference-time compute, and training signal. It's useful for best-of-n selection at test time, but it's also potentially a source of reward for domains where you don't have a clean verifier, like open-ended writing or messy real-world tasks, where you can't just check whether the math answer equals 42. That's where I think a lot of the open questions are right now: how far can you push LLM judges as a substitute for ground truth before things start to fall apart?

r001.rationale: The response says a judge can compare candidate chains of thought and identify coherent reasoning, skipped steps, and hallucinations, making the reasoning trajectory itself a basis for assessing validity.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've been thinking about a lot. The interesting thing is that when you sample multiple reasoning chains from a model, you very often get the right answer somewhere in there. Pass-at-k is usually way higher than pass-at-one. So the capability is kind of latent in the model, and the whole question becomes: how do you pick the right one?

The naive thing is majority voting, which works surprisingly well, but it's dumb in the sense that it only looks at the final answer. It throws away all the information in the reasoning itself. And it fails in a very specific way, which is that if the model has a systematic bias, the wrong answer can be the majority and you'll just confidently pick it.

So the LLM judge angle is interesting because the judge gets to actually read the chains. And there's this asymmetry that I find kind of beautiful, which is that verifying is often easier than generating. A model that can't reliably solve a problem in one shot can still look at five attempts and say, this one has a flaw in step three, this one actually checks out. It's a bit like how a reviewer doesn't need to be a better researcher than the author to find the bug in the proof.

The part that's genuinely not obvious to me, and this is where it gets fun, is whether the judge is actually doing verification or whether it's just pattern matching on surface features. Like, does it prefer the longer chain, the one that sounds more confident, the one that uses the right vocabulary? We know these biases exist in pairwise preference judging. Position bias, length bias, all of that. And when you're judging reasoning, those biases could be even more insidious because a wrong chain that's written fluently looks a lot like a right one.

The other thing that I think is underexplored is the compute tradeoff. If you're spending N samples on generation and then another big chunk of compute on judging, you have to ask whether that compute would have been better spent just making the base model better, or doing more samples with a cheap aggregator. My intuition is that the judge wins when the problem space is one where errors are detectable but solutions are hard to find, and it loses when the judge is basically as confused as the generator. And honestly, figuring out which regime you're in is most of the work.

And then there's the recursive thing, right, where you can use the judge's signal as a training signal, and then the judge and the policy are kind of co-evolving. That's where it starts to feel like the interesting frontier, but also where it gets scary, because if the judge has a blind spot, you're now optimizing directly into that blind spot.

r001.rationale: The response says the LLM judge reads the reasoning chains and checks them for flaws or whether they hold up, identifying chain-of-thought inspection as a basis for validity assessment.

astra-6.text:
I think the interesting thing is that generating a good answer and recognizing a good answer are different problems. If you sample multiple reasoning outputs, the model might get to the right answer in one of them, but you still need a way to select it. An LLM judge gives you a way to turn that diversity into a potentially better final answer.

But then the judge becomes the bottleneck. Can it actually distinguish correct reasoning from something that just sounds convincing? A longer, more polished explanation can be wrong. And if the judge shares the same blind spots as the model generating the answers, it might confidently pick the same mistake.

So what interests me is how much useful signal the judge adds. As you generate more candidates, does selection keep improving the result, or do you reach a point where the judge can’t tell them apart? That’s a really interesting question about how effectively we can use more computation at inference time.

r001.rationale: The response says a judge should distinguish correct reasoning from convincing but wrong reasoning, but it does not identify inspecting a trajectory’s chain of thought as the basis for that assessment.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the interesting thing is that generating a good answer and recognizing a good answer are different problems. If you sample multiple reasoning outputs, the model might get one of them right, but you still need a way to select it. So the judge becomes part of the reasoning system itself.

And then the question is: what is it actually judging? Is it checking correctness, or does it just prefer an answer that’s longer, more confident, or better written? A convincing explanation can still be wrong. So I think the exciting part is using that extra computation to improve selection, but you have to measure whether the judge can actually distinguish good reasoning from reasoning that merely looks good.
